The Three-Row Hot Rod That Refused to Die

How Dodge's "right-sized" family SUV survived an awkward second act, outlived fresher rivals, and became more relevant by stubbornly refusing to become sensible.

By Douglas James · Car Culture · Three Generations of Dodge Durango · 19 min read

The modern automobile industry has spent the past several years trying to convince us that cylinders are a character flaw. V8s have given way to turbocharged sixes, those sixes have surrendered to turbo fours, and the turbo fours have been wired to batteries, motors, generators and enough control modules to run a small regional airport. Physical buttons are vanishing, exhaust notes are being synthesized through the speakers, and even the humble family SUV now tends to arrive carrying a charging cable, an enormous screen, and a reassuring brochure explaining why its 2.0-liter engine is really all anyone could possibly need.

And then there is the Dodge Durango, which appears to have quietly skipped every one of those mandatory industry meetings. In its sixteenth model year, the current generation still offers a naturally aspirated V6, two naturally aspirated HEMI V8s, and a supercharged 6.2-liter V8 producing 710 horsepower. The 2026 range opens at $38,995, climbs through a 360-horsepower 5.7-liter HEMI and a 475-horsepower R/T 392, and finishes with the SRT Hellcat — an 8,700-pound-towing, three-row family vehicle that reaches 60 mph in roughly 3.5 seconds. It consumes gasoline with about the same restraint I show at an open bar: technically capable of stopping, philosophically opposed to the idea.

By every rule of the current market, this should be a car on life support. Instead it is thriving. Dodge sold 81,168 Durangos in 2025, a 37-percent jump over the year before and the nameplate's best calendar year since 2005, and that single elderly SUV accounted for nearly 80 percent of everything the Dodge brand sold. The momentum carried straight into 2026, with 20,300 leaving dealers in the first quarter alone — up 48 percent, the model's strongest opening quarter since 2021. The Durango is ancient by automotive standards, thirsty, heavy, and built on an architecture that dates to a time when the iPad was still a novelty. Somehow, all of that has curdled into an advantage.

To understand how a vehicle this out of step became this successful, you have to go back to the problem Dodge set out to solve in the first place — because the Durango has always made the most sense when everyone around it was zigging and it kept calmly zagging.

Before the Segment Had a Name

The Gap Nobody Else Had Spotted

In the late 1990s the SUV market had split into two increasingly separate camps. On one side sat the manageable models — the Ford Explorer, Chevrolet Blazer, Jeep Grand Cherokee and Toyota 4Runner — sensibly sized and priced, but generally short on passenger space, third-row availability, or serious towing muscle. On the other side loomed the giants: the Chevrolet Tahoe, Ford Expedition and Chevrolet Suburban, which offered all the room and capability you could want but were bigger, pricier, and considerably more cumbersome to live with. Between those two worlds lay a gap, and Dodge saw it clearly.

The company already had a template for splitting the difference. Its Dakota pickup occupied exactly that kind of middle ground between compact and full-size trucks, so the solution was elegantly straightforward: take the Dakota's basic truck foundation and build an SUV that was larger and more useful than the Explorer class but smaller and cheaper than a Tahoe. The first Durango arrived late in 1997 as a 1998 model, and it belonged to that rare category of product whose entire purpose you could grasp in a single glance. It seated up to eight, offered a proper third row, could be ordered with a V8, and could tow roughly 7,000 to 7,500 pounds when properly equipped.

The numbers made the pitch for it. At 193 inches long it stretched only 4.7 inches beyond the Explorer in a contemporary MotorTrend comparison, yet came in 6.4 inches shorter than a Tahoe — and in that same test it carried eight people to the Ford's five and swallowed 51.3 cubic feet of cargo against the Explorer's 42.6. Dodge called it "smart-sized." Today we would probably call it a segment buster, and either way the market understood it instantly.

First Generation

The Goldilocks SUV1998 – 2003

The first Durango was never elegant in the European sense. It looked as though a Dodge Dakota had gone to the gym, discovered protein powder, and decided to start a family — and that was exactly right. The pronounced fenders, the broad crosshair grille and the upright body made no attempt to disguise its truck origins, because it didn't need to. The Durango looked capable for the simple reason that it genuinely was.

The early engine menu was pure Dodge: a 5.2-liter Magnum V8, a larger 5.9-liter Magnum V8, and briefly a 3.9-liter V6 for buyers with gentler towing ambitions, before the newer 4.7-liter PowerTech V8 eventually replaced the 5.2. The 5.9 also powered the very first Durango R/T, planting a small but consequential seed — the idea that a three-row family hauler could carry genuine hot-rod character. Nobody knew it at the time, but that seed would define the nameplate two decades later.

It still drove like a truck, and the reviews said so. The ride could be stiff, the steering was hardly delicate, the brakes drew criticism, and the long body was no enthusiast's off-road companion; Consumer Reports flagged the trucklike handling and choppy ride even while acknowledging the usefulness of that folding third row. But those complaints were beside the point. The first Durango handed families a great deal more utility without shoving them into a full-size SUV — it could haul children, grandparents, camping gear and a trailer without occupying an entire suburban ZIP code — and it arrived at precisely the right cultural moment.

Second Generation

The Difficult Second Album2004 – 2009

Every successful vehicle eventually gets a sequel, and not every sequel is The Empire Strikes Back. The second-generation Durango was closer to the kind of follow-up where the whole cast returns, the budget balloons, the explosions get bigger, and somewhere in all the spectacle the original magic quietly goes missing. Introduced for 2004, the redesign grew in nearly every dimension — stretching to roughly 200.8 inches on a 119.2-inch wheelbase, opening up an enormous 102.4 cubic feet of maximum cargo room, and, when properly equipped, towing as much as 8,700 pounds, a figure normally reserved for far larger machinery.

The engine range stayed reassuringly Dodge-like: a 3.7-liter V6 for entry models, a 4.7-liter V8, and the newly available 5.7-liter HEMI making an initial 335 horsepower. The HEMI was the headline act, delivering effortless acceleration, serious trailer-hauling ability, and an identity that no amount of unfortunate dashboard plastic could entirely erase. The problem was that there turned out to be a great deal of unfortunate dashboard plastic.

Styling is always subjective, but the second-generation Durango made subjectivity work overtime. Where the first model looked muscular and compact for its capability, the second simply looked swollen — a bigger grille, headlights that seemed to have migrated up and out, and flanks that gave the impression the bodywork had been inflated moments before the photographer arrived. Inside, it got worse. The dashboard looked as though it had been negotiated between an accountant, a plastics supplier, and someone who had once had a pickup-truck interior described to them over the telephone. The materials were hard, the shapes were blocky, and the general atmosphere suggested Rubbermaid had narrowly lost the interior contract.

None of which made it a bad tool. It remained spacious, quiet enough, powerful and hugely capable, and contemporary reviews genuinely admired the HEMI and its towing. But the criticisms were hard to wave away — Consumer Reports recorded just 12 mpg overall from its HEMI test car and called the fit and finish subpar — and the Durango had, in the space of one redesign, gained capability while losing charm. Worse, the ground was shifting beneath it. Buyers were streaming toward car-based crossovers like the Honda Pilot, Toyota Highlander, Mazda CX-9 and Chevrolet Traverse, which offered three rows, easier step-in, more carlike manners and better economy. A lot of families were discovering that they loved the space and image of an SUV but had no particular need for a truck frame or the ability to drag a mobile home out of a swamp. The Durango stayed a traditional SUV at the precise moment traditional SUVs became hard to sell.

Then the 2008 financial crisis arrived, vehicle demand collapsed, and fuel prices lurched around violently. Dodge's response was technically fascinating: the 2009 Durango Hybrid paired the 5.7-liter HEMI with two electric motors and a sophisticated two-mode hybrid transmission developed through an industry partnership, producing around 385 horsepower while returning roughly 21 mpg combined — genuinely impressive for a big V8 SUV of the era. It was also expensive, complex, and launched at the exact moment both Chrysler's finances and the large-SUV market were caving in. The hybrid wasn't so much ahead of its time as briefly visible while the building was being evacuated.

Third Generation

The Reinvention2011 – present

When the Durango returned for 2011, it abandoned the pickup-derived body-on-frame construction that had defined it from the start. That could have read as surrender. Instead it turned out to be liberation. The new car adopted unitized construction and shared a significant chunk of its underbody with the contemporary Jeep Grand Cherokee, but it held onto rear-wheel-drive proportions and available V8 power while transforming its ride, handling, steering, refinement and interior quality. The Durango had become a crossover in its bones without becoming the least bit apologetic about it.

The standard 3.6-liter Pentastar V6 made 290 horsepower, while the optional 5.7-liter HEMI delivered 360 horsepower and 390 pound-feet of torque and, properly equipped, towed 7,400 pounds — more than most three-row crossovers could dream of — with rear- or all-wheel drive on the menu. Most importantly, the third generation simply looked good. The roof sat lower, the body was cleaner, and the proportions turned athletic, planted where the previous car had looked swollen. The rear-drive architecture allowed a longer hood and a stance closer to an oversized sport wagon than a conventional family box. If the second generation looked like it was carrying too much water, the third looked like it had been carrying dumbbells.

It did not, however, begin life as the outrageous performance machine we know now. That identity arrived in stages, each one turning the wick up a little further, until a school-run SUV had quietly become one of the most unhinged things on the new-car market.

How a Family SUV Became a Muscle Car

The Slow Descent Into Madness

The first real step came in 2014, when Dodge revised the styling and fitted an eight-speed automatic that sharpened acceleration, refinement and efficiency while making far better use of both the Pentastar and the HEMI. The Durango stopped being merely a competent three-row SUV and started becoming distinctly, recognizably Dodge. Then came 2018 and the arrival of the SRT, which dropped in the 6.4-liter, 392-cubic-inch HEMI — 475 horsepower, 470 pound-feet, all-wheel drive, 60 mph in about 4.4 seconds, and still an 8,700-pound tow rating. This was the moment the Durango stopped pretending to be a normal family vehicle. With Brembo brakes, adaptive dampers, performance drive modes, enormous tires and an exhaust note capable of ending neighborhood conversations several houses away, the SRT was what happened when a school-run SUV ate a muscle car and decided it liked the taste. It could still carry three rows of passengers and a week of groceries; it simply did so with the demeanor of a getaway vehicle.

And then, in 2021, Dodge installed the supercharged 6.2-liter Hellcat V8, apparently having concluded that the 475-horsepower version was creating dangerous shortages of absurdity. The Durango SRT Hellcat made 710 horsepower and 645 pound-feet, hit 60 mph in roughly 3.5 seconds, and — because this remained, nominally, a family SUV — kept the full 8,700-pound towing capacity. The same update brought a redesigned dashboard and an available 10.1-inch Uconnect 5 system, finally giving the aging architecture a genuinely modern cabin. A 710-horsepower three-row SUV is not a rational transportation solution. It is a parent-teacher conference conducted by artillery.

For 2026, Dodge initially signaled that the Durango would go all-V8 — then reconsidered and restored the Pentastar V6 in November 2025, presumably after remembering that some buyers need to move children without refinancing the house at every fuel stop. The result may be the most complete Durango lineup yet, with the 392 now standard in the R/T for the first time, promising a claimed 4.4-second 0–60 and a 12.9-second quarter-mile for under $50,000 before options. It is a genuinely remarkable spread: a family can buy a reasonably priced V6, a boat owner can step up to the 5.7 HEMI, an enthusiast can choose the 392, and someone who believes the school drop-off lane ought to require a parachute can sign for the Hellcat — all of them wearing the same handsome bodywork.

Those totals reward a second look. The supposedly obsolete current car has already outsold the entire second generation by more than two to one, and it is closing in on the original's lifetime total despite operating in a vastly more crowded market. Across all three generations, more than two million Durangos have now found homes. Which raises the obvious question: how on earth is an eleven-years-unchanged, V8-guzzling dinosaur pulling this off in 2026?

Why Does This Old Thing Still Work?

Six Reasons the Dinosaur Thrives

The easy answer is that Americans love V8s, and that is true as far as it goes — but it is also incomplete, because most Durangos sold are not Hellcats, and the humble V6 has always accounted for a meaningful slice of the volume. The fuller explanation is that almost every part of the package still occupies a genuinely useful position, and that several of the car's supposed weaknesses have quietly turned into strengths.

The first reason is that it still sits neatly between two classes, exactly as the original did. The current car is more substantial, more rear-drive-biased and more tow-capable than most family crossovers, yet less enormous and usually less expensive than full-size body-on-frame SUVs like the Tahoe, Expedition and Wagoneer. At 85.1 cubic feet of maximum cargo capacity it is useful without being class-leading, and its third row is perfectly usable without being the roomiest in the segment. Its real advantage was never winning any single interior measurement; it is that Dodge pairs adequate family space with capability that similarly priced crossovers simply cannot match — more than 50 seating configurations, room for up to seven, and up to 8,700 pounds of towing. The Durango remains a middleweight that can punch clean into the heavyweight division, and dealers will happily tell you it cross-shops against vehicles a full size class above it.

The second reason is actual mechanical choice. Where many rivals offer a single engine in one or two states of tune, the Durango offers four distinct personalities — the sensible V6, the sonorous 5.7, the seriously quick 392, and the frankly antisocial Hellcat. That range lets one vehicle serve wildly different budgets and temperaments without diluting its character, because a base Durango still looks unmistakably related to the Hellcat, sharing its stance and attitude. The performance models don't feel like unrelated halo cars bolted onto a generic SUV; they elevate the whole range, and a little of the Hellcat's menace rubs off on every trim below it.

The third reason is the least glamorous and possibly the most important: the platform has been paid for. Stellantis doesn't publish the program's development costs, so this can't be proven from the accounts, but it is reasonable to infer that an architecture in production for more than fifteen years has had the overwhelming majority of its engineering and tooling investment amortized many times over. That gives Dodge room to keep refreshing the electronics, interior, trim and powertrains without funding an all-new platform every six years. A newer competitor often has to recover billions spent on fresh architecture, emissions compliance, electrification and software; the Durango can turn up with a familiar engine, a familiar transmission, and an assembly process refined over a decade and a half. Old engineering can be a liability, but paid-off engineering becomes pricing power — and pricing power is exactly how the Durango stays the cheapest V8 SUV on the market while still updating what customers touch and see.

Old engineering can be a liability. Paid-off engineering becomes pricing power.

The fourth reason is that familiarity itself has quietly become a luxury. There was a time when an old-school interior simply felt dated; now, in a market where some cabins feel like consumer electronics with wheels, a car you can operate without a tutorial feels reassuring. The Durango has a modern touchscreen and up-to-date connectivity, but it keeps recognizable buttons and physical controls for the things that matter — you don't dive into a submenu to change the temperature or negotiate with a glowing panel to warm a seat. That doesn't make it primitive. It makes it legible, and legibility has become genuinely rare.

The fifth reason is that the Durango has no identity crisis whatsoever. It isn't pretending to be an off-road lifestyle accessory, or trying to resemble a coupe, or presenting itself as a minimalist Scandinavian wellness retreat, or asking to be admired for its environmental virtue. It is a roomy, powerful, rear-drive-based family SUV that can tow a large trailer and make a magnificent noise, and both the car and its buyers know it. That consistency has built a kind of trust that most of the market has forfeited: a Durango shopper never has to wonder whether Dodge has secretly turned it into a front-drive four-cylinder crossover wearing a familiar badge. The old dog keeps doing its old tricks because people keep paying to watch them.

The sixth reason is the one Dodge can take the least credit for: the competition has largely vacated the territory. The Ford Expedition has moved to turbocharged V6 power, the latest Explorer leans heavily on turbo four- and six-cylinder engines, and much of the three-row field now emphasizes hybrids, smaller displacement and electrification. Those products may well be quicker, cleaner, more efficient or more sophisticated — but every departure from the traditional V8 SUV leaves the Durango with less direct competition. Dodge didn't so much conquer the segment as watch everyone else walk out of it, and then keep the lights on.

The Elephant Drinking at the Bar

About That Fuel Bill

None of this makes the Durango's thirst an amusing footnote, and it would be dishonest to pretend otherwise. The Hellcat carries EPA estimates of around 12 mpg city, 17 highway and 13 combined, and even the 5.7-liter HEMI is a thirsty thing next to newer turbo and hybrid rivals. Fuel is expensive, too, though it's worth being precise rather than dramatic about it: as of mid-July 2026 the U.S. average for regular gasoline sat around $3.86 a gallon, with the West Coast closer to $4.83 and California above $5.00. Those are painful numbers, particularly in California — but they remain below the inflation-adjusted peaks of earlier fuel crises, so describing them as an all-time national record wouldn't quite be accurate.

There's a nuance in the sales story, as well. The Durango hasn't defied economics by climbing in a straight line — sales actually slid 14 percent in 2024 before rebounding 37 percent in 2025, and while the first quarter of 2026 was spectacular, second-quarter volume slipped 12 percent year over year, with the first half staying positive largely because that opening surge was so strong. This isn't magic, in other words. It's simply proof that enough buyers still value what the Durango offers to accept its running costs with clear eyes. The person signing for a Hellcat is not going to discover 13-mpg economy after the paperwork clears; they walked into the dealership already understanding that this vehicle treats premium fuel less like a resource and more like a subscription service.

It Doesn't Win Everything

And Doesn't Need To

The Durango rarely dominates a conventional comparison test, and it's fair to say why. Newer rivals may offer better fuel economy, more advanced driver-assistance systems, larger third rows, more cargo room behind the last seat, smoother hybrid powertrains, newer structural engineering and more polished interiors, and the Durango's age can genuinely be felt in its packaging and electronics — a refreshed dashboard can only do so much to disguise an architecture developed during the first Obama administration. But the notion that it never finishes first isn't quite fair either. The Durango ranked first among upper-midsize SUVs in the 2025 J.D. Power APEAL Study, which measures how much owners actually love and enjoy their vehicles across dozens of attributes — and that particular distinction is revealing.

It may not win the spreadsheet, but its owners enjoy it, and that gets closer to the heart of the thing than any cargo figure. There are plenty of objectively excellent SUVs that inspire no affection whatsoever — quiet, efficient, safe, competent machines their owners appreciate in roughly the way they appreciate a well-functioning refrigerator. The Durango has flaws you can list and a personality you can feel, and in 2026 that turns out to be a surprisingly rare and valuable combination.

The Brand's Accidental Lifeboat

The Car Carrying All of Dodge

The Durango's recent strength also has to be read against the state of Dodge itself, because the context is genuinely startling. The Challenger and the previous Charger ended production after 2023, their replacements arrived slowly and initially leaned heavily on electric power, and the Hornet has struggled to build sustained volume. Against that backdrop, Dodge sold 101,927 vehicles in the United States in 2025 — and more than 81,000 of them were Durangos. A vehicle introduced for 2011 now represents roughly 80 percent of its entire brand's U.S. sales.

That is at once impressive and a little unsettling. The Durango isn't merely Dodge's veteran contributor; it is carrying the team, driving the bus, and apparently running the refreshment stand at halftime. Its strength proves there is real, durable demand for what it does — but it also lays bare how dependent Dodge has become on a product that, by every normal rule of the industry, ought to have been replaced years ago.

The Next One

How Do You Replace This?

Stellantis has confirmed investment tied to the Durango's future, and as of a mid-2026 investor update the plan points toward a comprehensive refresh rather than an all-new redesign in the near term, with a genuinely next-generation car expected further out. Either way, it creates a fascinating problem: how do you replace a vehicle whose single greatest attribute is that it has stubbornly resisted being replaced? A truly new Durango will have to meet stricter emissions and safety rules, will almost certainly bring more sophisticated electronics, and may well adopt electrified power; it will need better efficiency, improved packaging and newer driver-assistance technology.

The trap Dodge has to avoid is engineering away the very reasons people still buy it. The next Durango cannot become just another smooth, turbocharged, three-row crossover with a big screen and an old name; to work, it needs to keep the rear-drive character, the substantial towing, the accessible pricing, the strong visual identity, the mechanical variety, and some genuine measure of Dodge excess. A Durango that lost its sense of humor would be a real loss. And since the current car is expected to soldier on until its successor is ready, this generation could ultimately approach two full decades in production — at which rate the final examples may nearly qualify for historic registration while still sitting in dealer inventory.

The Real Reason It Endures

It Knew What It Was

Strip away the horsepower wars and the sales charts, and the Durango endures for one unfashionable reason: it stayed loyal to its original purpose. The first generation existed to offer more room, seating and towing than an Explorer or Grand Cherokee without demanding the size and cost of a Tahoe or Expedition. The second generation briefly lost that balance, growing larger, heavier and less attractive just as the market pivoted to crossovers. The third generation found the formula again — the useful middle size of the original, now wrapped in better road manners, a handsome body, a vastly improved cabin, and the performance identity of Dodge's muscle cars.

And then Dodge did the genuinely unusual thing. It stopped reinventing the car and started refining it instead. An eight-speed transmission, better electronics, a new dashboard, more safety equipment, the SRT, the Hellcat, the Tow 'n Go package, the return of the 392 — the architecture stayed put while the personality intensified. That is why the Durango has become an anomaly rather than a relic. Its age is no longer merely evidence of neglect; it has become evidence that the underlying idea was unusually sound to begin with.

The Durango is not the newest SUV, nor the most efficient, the most spacious, the most technologically advanced or the most refined. It is something increasingly rare, which is honest. It is a three-row family SUV with enough room for daily life, enough capability for serious work, and a spread of engines that runs from perfectly reasonable to completely deranged — starting below $40,000, towing 8,700 pounds, carrying seven people, and, in Hellcat form, accelerating as though it has just remembered the children are late and the school sits at the far end of a drag strip.

It has survived three generations, an economic crisis, Chrysler's bankruptcy, several corporate mergers, the crossover revolution, the rise of the EV, the retreat of the V8, and very nearly every major shift in modern automotive fashion. It has never been the teacher's favorite and it rarely turns up in the latest clothes. It drinks too much, speaks too loudly, and occasionally behaves in ways that alarm the neighbors. But it keeps showing up — and after nearly three decades, the reason it keeps outliving its competitors may be wonderfully simple. It understood what it was from the very beginning, and after one unfortunate makeover, it remembered.

Everyone else read the room and left. The Durango stayed at the bar, ordered another round, and somehow closed the place down still standing.
